paragraphs.text: Red-white ( or RW ), also called Boros , is an enemy color pair. Their central conflict is freedom ( red ) vs. security ( white ). Red-white lends itself to aggro decks . The two colors share the evergreen keywords first strike , double strike , and flying . They are mutual allies of green ( ).

The central conflict between red and white is freedom vs. security. Red wants everyone to be allowed to act as they feel; white wants to keep everyone safe through laws and other structures. Red views this conflict as freedom vs. fascism; white views it as chaos vs. order. Red-white characters typically fall into one of two categories: seeking justice outside the law (white ends, red means), or using the law and other social structures to create chaos (red ends, white means).

Red-white is the most passionate and idealistic color pair, combining red's emotional drive with white's zealotry. Its strong beliefs make it honest and blunt. Red-white is also the most loving color pair, an overlap between red's passion and white's desire to see everyone safe and happy. And it is the fastest and most action-oriented; red and white are both associated with trained fighters.

Above all, red-white wants to do the right thing. It acts for the good of society, although it obeys the spirit of the law more than the letter. It also seeks to prevent unnecessary change, which it shares in common with green , its overlapping ally. At its worst, red-white is the color pair of rationalization : it can always justify its own impulses as morally correct. And it can be so headstrong and focused on its goal that it ignores other concerns.
Examples of red-white heroes include Agrus Kos and Quintorius Kand , while villains include Nahiri and Risona .

Red-white lends itself to aggro decks . White has the most efficient cheap creatures , while red is the best at getting blockers out of the way and pushing through damage . The two colors diverge at higher mana values , where red becomes more destructive and white becomes more defensive. Designing expensive red-white can therefore be difficult. Red-white Limited archetypes are usually aggressive, not because the color pair can't branch out, but because sets need an aggressive archetype and red-white is best suited to it.
